extracted.intended_audience: administrative law scholars, tribunal administrators, policymakers, and lawyers working on social security appeals (Canada)
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive and evaluative analysis of the practice, procedure, jurisdiction, composition, and decision-making of the Pension Appeal Board (PAB) and the Social Affairs Commission (SAC), with attention to access, remedies, timeliness, and judicial-review implications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight of medical evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The PAB could hardly attach the same weight to a certificate simply signed by the beneficiary's family doctor as to one supported by the physician's oral evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Written medical reports are often elliptical and may be inclined in favour of the patient; oral evidence from examining physicians is viewed as stronger. The tribunal treats certificates from family doctors with less weight than oral testimony from the examining specialist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minister's access to expert medical evidence at hearings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Minister of National Health and Welfare invariably has a physician attached to the Disability Assessment Division in attendance at the hearing; if possible, one of the Division physicians who took part in the examination of the case in the first place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the Minister can produce Division physicians or medical specialists as witnesses, the Minister is positioned to offer expert evidence supporting his interpretation of medical findings — a factor that affects evidentiary balance at hearings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Language access and interpreter provision
rubrics_metrics.description: PAB members can hear appeals in either official language; where a defendant or third party is obviously incapable of testifying in English or in French, it is up to the Minister to provide, at his own expense, the services of an interpreter in appeals lodged by the Minister. When the appeal is initiated by the beneficiary, interpretation costs are to be charged to the beneficiary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguishes obligations depending on who initiates the appeal; practical impact on recent immigrants and construction workers who may be unable to express themselves adequately. Interpreter costs allocation affects access to fair hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reimbursement for travel allowances and legal expenses (section 88 CPP)
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 88 differentiates between: (1) payment of travelling and other allowances including compensation for loss of remuneration to a party implicated in an appeal if requested by the PAB to take part and does so; and (2) repayment of legal expenses (lawyer's fees) to a 'respondent' beneficiary or second claimant summoned to appear, but only if actually represented by a lawyer at the hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Travel/loss-of-remuneration compensation is available to beneficiaries who can establish incurred expenses or income loss due to participation. Legal-fee reimbursement requires being a respondent/second claimant and actual lawyer representation. The Registrar notifies potentially eligible parties when the hearing date is set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision formalities: written reasons and communication
rubrics_metrics.description: The Acts require that decisions rendered by the Board shall be in writing, have reasons assigned to them, and be communicated to the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usual practice: judges deliberate, designate one member to draft reasons; the majority opinion constitutes the decision; the signed draft is forwarded to the Registrar who prepares the formal judgment and sends it with reasons to parties. Rarely are decisions delivered orally at the hearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and deliberation practice for issuing decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The PAB very seldom hands down decisions at the time of the hearing; more usual is rendering judgment after a period of deliberation with a draft prepared and circulated to colleagues for approval and signature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Average time between hearing and delivery in the sample: 30 days for benefits cases and 80 days for contributions cases. Contributions cases typically require more elaborate decisions due to greater factual and legal complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of caselaw in decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: The PAB makes fairly abundant use of caselaw in its decisions: not only of its own but also of that developed by the regular courts, especially in connection with the characterization of work relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliance on precedent is an explicit part of the Board's reasoning process and affects outcome consistency and predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of appellate powers (affirm, vacate, vary, refer)
rubrics_metrics.description: The PAB is empowered to affirm, vacate or vary the decision challenged by appeal and claims the power to refer certain questions it does not consider to be its own responsibility to subordinate authorities for disposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outcome categories include affirmations, variations, vacaturs, referrals, ratifications of settlements, and withdrawals; the Board's statutory powers define the remedial options available on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical analysis of appeal outcomes and causal interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Beneficiaries tend to win their cases, at least in part, almost as often as the Minister. The relatively high success rate of beneficiaries may largely be due to the Minister's withdrawal of some appeals, or his willingness to settle before the hearing. Trends noted include increased litigation concerning the surviving spouse's pension and growth in beneficiaries' success rate coinciding with more critical Review Committees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outcome statistics should be interpreted in light of withdrawals, settlements, types of cases, and changes in Review Committee attitudes; 'split decisions' that fix onset mid-way between claims are another outcome pattern to consider.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficiency and duration of appeals process
rubrics_metrics.description: Litigation concerning CPP benefits may drag on for little less than three years; contributions-related cases have fewer levels of appeal but waiting periods between phases offset efficiency gains.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiplicity of appeal authorities lengthens the sequence and slows disposal of benefit-related appeals. Time-interval analysis between procedural phases is a metric of tribunal effectiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial-review status and clarity of review avenues
rubrics_metrics.description: The PAB is expressly excluded from the judicial review authority of the Federal Court of Appeal under section 28(6) of the Federal Court Act, but is not exempt from the review jurisdiction of the Federal Court under section 18; the exact status and available remedies remain uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions discussed include whether PAB falls within 'federal tribunal' definitions, persona designata doctrine for judges appointed under federal statutes, the effect of statutory exceptions on the Trial Division's jurisdiction, and whether remedies under section 18 revive when section 28(6) precludes section 28(1) applications. The uncertainty has practical significance for avenues of challenge (e.g., certiorari, prohibition, writs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Advantage of constitutive statute for mapping jurisdiction (SAC)
rubrics_metrics.description: The jurisdiction of the SAC is completely mapped out in section 20 of its constitutive statute, which enumerates 22 areas of authority; a constitutive statute provides a complete and consistent picture of organization and functioning and is preferable to the method used to establish the PAB.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using a dedicated statute to create a tribunal yields clarity about scope, powers, and procedures across its multiple jurisdictions, improving coherence and predictability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth and clarity of SAC jurisdiction (enumerated categories)
rubrics_metrics.description: Eight broad categories of decisions may be appealed to the SAC: decisions concerning monetary benefits; benefits in kind; authorization to exercise an occupation or carry on a business; access to welfare or health files; personal freedom; complaints concerning quality of services provided by certain public establishments; payment of professional services; and elections or appointments to managing bodies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first category (monetary benefits) is most extensive and covers appeals under many Acts (Social Aid Act, Quebec Family Allowances Plan, Quebec Pension Plan, Workmen's Compensation Act, etc.). Clear categorization supports assignment of expertise and procedural design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for member versatility and technical expertise
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions appealed to the SAC are extremely varied in nature and their settlement calls for very diverse forms of expertise; the exercise of such multifarious powers demands a correspondingly high degree of versatility of SAC members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Composition and organization of the Commission are intended to ensure versatility—initially by appointing physicians (including a psychiatrist) and lawyers, and later structuring members and assessors to combine legal and technical expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition rules and role of assessors (SAC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial Bill: membership (no more than nine) with at least two physicians and one lawyer; after amendments, distinction between members (eight lawyers, president and vice-president chosen among them) and assessors; president may be judge; president, vice-president and at least one other member to devote themselves exclusively to duties; terms not exceeding ten years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amendments responded to Bar objections that tribunals should consist of jurists while retaining technical expertise via assessors; recruitment difficulties for qualified staff were noted. Composition rules affect perceptions of fairness, legal competence, and technical capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy objectives behind tribunal centralization (rationale for SAC)
rubrics_metrics.description: Four considerations for creating the SAC: (1) concentrate in a single tribunal all appeals against administrative decisions within the sector served by the Department of Social Affairs; (2) broaden some of the remedies available and create an administrative authority of high accessibility to hear these remedies; (3) introduce uniformity into procedures applicable to various types of remedy; (4) entrust the Commission to work out a coherent and accessible caselaw in the social security sector.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Centralization aimed to improve access, uniformity, remedy breadth, and caselaw coherence; ministerial rationale also included relieving PAB overload to protect beneficiaries' access to appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shared jurisdiction with ordinary courts on access-to-records appeals
rubrics_metrics.description: The SAC's authority to hear appeals by persons denied access to their social or medical records is one that it shares with various ordinary courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Overlap requires attention to forum choice, potential duplication, and harmonization of standards between administrative and ordinary courts.
